item.title: Newly discovered amoeba reproduces at 145 F, breaking heat record for eukaryotic life
item.description: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Planetary collisions may help young worlds hold on to their atmospheres
item.description: A new study lets some of the air out of a long-held theory that growing, rocky planets will lose their atmosphere if they smash into a large object in space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3,700-year-old man buried with stone in his mouth beneath a hearth may have been part of magical ritual
item.description: Approximately 3,700 years ago, a man in southeastern Spain underwent a burial unlike any other. Researchers suggest that this ritual may have been intended to symbolically overcome a threat rather than inflict punishment. The discovery of his body underneath a hearth, with a stone in his mouth, implies an effort to silence him. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Fresh as the microplastic-laden Sierra snow: Storms can deliver pollution to even remote locations
item.description: For the first time, UC Riverside scientists have measured how much microplastic pollution falls on the Sierra Nevada during snowstorms and were surprised to find significant amounts even in the most remote locations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light reshapes gelatin scaffolds to steer cell growth in three dimensions
item.description: Soft, flexible hydrogels have enabled significant advancements in engineering biological tissue by mimicking the natural scaffolding that provides structure and support to cells. Existing engineered hydrogels, however, fall short in a significant way. Unlike in nature, they do not have the dynamic ability to change their structure or support depending on what the biological tissue needs. The answer may rest in shining a light on the problem—literally, according to a team led by researchers at Yokohama National University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture
item.description: Research on political polarization points to how people's preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The rugged summits of the Cordillera del Paine mountain range pierce the sky in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile.
item.description: The rugged summits of the Cordillera del Paine mountain range pierce the sky in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile. The Cliffs of Insanity, but with a much better view. Inconceivable that this is real! HomeownerPal Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Experimental study on moths supports the molecular cookie cutter idea proposed for butterflies
item.description: Have you ever thought about reinventing yourself? According to a new study on moths conducted by Andrei Sourakov, collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida, it's not as hard as you might think. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is it a boy or a girl? For alligators, it may come down to one degree
item.description: The future of the alligator species could come down to a one- or two-degree temperature difference, according to new research from the University of Georgia. The findings are published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A blue laser for underwater communication and sensing
item.description: Researchers at EPFL have developed a chip-scale blue laser that combines stable light emission with rapid frequency control, opening possibilities for underwater communication, environmental sensing and quantum technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Built to take the blast: Students test prototype landing pad to make moon landings safer
item.description: As NASA works toward a sustained human presence on the moon, researchers at The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH), a part of The University of Alabama System, are helping solve one of the most pressing challenges facing future lunar missions: how to land spacecraft safely without damaging the landing vehicle or nearby infrastructure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Key Atlantic currents could collapse this century, but the risk is missing from almost all national climate plans
item.description: Icelandic government officials recently met to discuss a dramatic scenario: what if the current that circulates Atlantic waters weakened significantly, or collapsed altogether? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Famed oceanographer calls for ending krill catch near Antarctica as governments debate fishing quota
item.description: Renowned oceanographer Sylvia Earle is calling for an end to krill fishing near Antarctica as officials from the U.S., China, Russia and 24 other governments negotiate a possible deal to dramatically expand fishing for the crustacean that's a vital food source for whales in the international waters surrounding the ice-covered continent. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nighttime songs could reveal when endangered pygmy blue whales feed off Western Australia
item.description: Listening to the songs of endangered pygmy blue whales could help researchers identify when the animals are feeding off Western Australia's coast, improving scientists' ability to monitor their behavior and inform conservation efforts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
item.description: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett

item.title: Researchers create first whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate
item.description: Viewed from above, Danionella cerebrum offers a rare sight in a vertebrate: its brain, visible through the top of its head. Since the species was adopted for neuroscience research in 2018 and formally described in 2021, the tiny, transparent fish has drawn rapidly growing interest for its unique biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Birds and humans share fundamental song and speech patterns, study finds
item.description: McGill University researchers have identified "universal" vocal patterns across hundreds of bird species and found that many of the same patterns also appear in human song and speech from cultures around the world. The patterns include small pitch intervals, regular and predictable rhythms, and phrase-final elongation, in which the last utterance in a phrase tends to be longer than the others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors
item.description: A study led by Oxford University has found that seabirds flying long distances across the Atlantic can experience a mismatch between their internal body clocks and local time (the same process that leads to jet lag in humans), causing them to make predictable errors when navigating by the sun. The results have been published in the journal Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
item.description: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lauren E. Low

item.title: Analysis of Córdoba's urban trees identifies which species best tolerate heat
item.description: The orange tree emerges as one of the most heat-vulnerable trees, according to a University of Córdoba (UCO) study that analyzed 17 tree species found in Córdoba's urban environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global maps reveal farming, dams and agricultural runoff as leading threats to freshwater species
item.description: Farming, dams and agricultural runoff are the biggest threats to freshwater biodiversity globally, with Europe and Northwest Africa the hardest-hit regions, McGill researchers have found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI helps uncover overlooked 2D materials and create 11 new ones
item.description: With the help of artificial intelligence, researchers at Linköping University in Sweden have found previously overlooked occurrences of the 2D materials MXenes in older databases. The findings have inspired the researchers to create new materials using more sustainable synthesis methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One molecule, many atoms: Platinum bonds respond to surface features up to 10 nanometers away
item.description: Many chemical processes that sustain modern society depend on molecules binding to metal surfaces. The production of synthetic fertilizer, for example, relies on heterogeneous catalysis, in which gases react on the surface of a solid catalyst. Yet, until now, an important question has remained unresolved: How much of the metal surface actually participates in determining the strength of a chemical bond on the surface? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NIH–NASA QuSAFE Challenge
item.description: The Quantum-Enabled Predictive Preclinical NAMs for Toxicity and Safety (QuSAFE) Challenge, a collaboration between the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and NASA, advances quantum-enabled sensing for in vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), to improve drug safety while reducing animal use. In vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), can […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Bailey Light

item.title: Unusual whale sightings around Australia may signal changing ocean conditions
item.description: Whales never cease to amaze me. After nearly two decades of studying these majestic mammals, I've learned every whale season is slightly different. Each migration along Australia's east coast varies in its timing and the number of whale sightings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly characterized Streptomyces strain yields previously unknown natural products
item.description: In a collaboration, researchers from the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures and the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) have discovered two previously unknown natural products. Lavasamycin A and B are produced by the bacterium Streptomyces barkulensis subsp. lavasanensis, which was isolated from a soil sample collected in Lavasan, Iran, and characterized as a new subspecies at the DSMZ. The findings have been published in the Journal of Natural Products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shrinking bat populations can weaken ecosystem benefits even while species remain widespread
item.description: Bats promote the health of ecosystems in many ways. Insect-eating species help regulate insect populations, including agricultural and forest pests. In tropical and subtropical regions, nectar-feeding and fruit-eating bats pollinate plants and disperse seeds, supporting plant reproduction and forest regeneration. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and cockroach zombies: The animal versions of our Halloween horrors
item.description: Around this time of year, elaborate decorations featuring ghosts, vampires, zombies, witches and werewolves adorn front doors, gardens and store windows across the country. But you may be surprised to hear that in the animal world, there are many real-life creatures with tendencies similar to those of the fictional characters in our Halloween nightmares. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Data centers could send US climate pollution skyrocketing
item.description: The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. That would essentially wipe out 15 years of greenhouse gas reductions. CO2 […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Justine Calma

item.title: Africa's water availability sometimes goes untapped
item.description: Water demand in Africa grew by around 26% between 2010 and 2020, yet around 717 million people lacked a piped water supply in 2020, according to research published in Nature. The findings indicate that water scarcity in some parts of Africa may be due to a lack of infrastructure, rather than a lack of available water. The work provides a comprehensive map for water demand in different sectors, highlighting issues that need to be addressed to increase the availability of water in Africa, which forms part of Sustainable Development Goal 6. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1987, an amateur fossil hunter found a T. rex in South Dakota; the $31.8 million skeleton now stands in Abu Dhabi
item.description: In 1987, Stan Sacrison found a T. rex skeleton in South Dakota, which was later sold for $31.8 million. Initially misidentified, the bones were correctly recognized as belonging to a T. rex in 1992. After years at the Black Hills Institute, the skeleton was auctioned and purchased for a museum in Abu Dhabi. Stan is now displayed in a dramatic scene depicting conflicts with another T. rex. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: How stealth partisan outlets exploit trust in local journalism
item.description: New research from Carnegie Mellon University's Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science found that partisan media operations spent millions of dollars on social media ads ahead of key elections to promote pink slime websites masquerading as local news sources to sway voters with their content. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rubin observatory reveals two hidden companions of the Milky Way
item.description: Preview data from the recently completed NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile point to a wave of discoveries that may complete the census of the Milky Way's neighboring galaxies—including its faintest companions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why people turn a blind eye to prisoner abuse
item.description: Common beliefs that people who commit crime are inherently bad and unlikely to change may make the public more accepting of illegitimate harms within the criminal justice system, according to criminology and psychology experts in the U.S. and Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat-evolved algae offer clues to helping corals withstand warming seas
item.description: A research team led by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) has found that heat-evolved algae maintain more stable biomolecular profiles under elevated temperatures than their non-evolved (wild-type) counterparts, providing new insights into how they withstand heat stress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La ESA y China ya tienen su primera imagen completa de la aurora boreal. Y no se parece a ninguna que hayas visto
item.description: Hay muchas formas de ver una aurora. Puede ser boreal o austral, según el hemisferio desde el que la observes. La puedes ver cerca de los polos, donde es más habitual, o en latitudes medias si la actividad solar es tan alta que lo permite. Generalmente las vemos desde la superficie terrestre, aunque algunos astronautas han logrado verlas desde el espacio. Incluso se han visto auroras en otros planetas. Pero, sin duda, nadie había visto las auroras como las ha mostrado recientemente la misión SMILE , fruto de la colaboración entre China y la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA). Anillo auroral… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Envía tu nombre a Titán a bordo de la misión Dragonfly de la NASA
item.description: Read this release in English here. Puede que nunca llegues a surcar los cielos bajo las nubes o sobre las arenas orgánicas de la luna Titán de Saturno, ¡pero tu nombre sí puede hacerlo! La NASA invita al público a enviar su nombre a bordo de la aeronave de ala giratoria Dragonfly de la agencia […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: María José Viñas

item.title: Send Your Name to Titan Aboard NASA’s Dragonfly Mission
item.description: You may never soar under the clouds or over the organic sands of Saturn’s moon Titan, but your name can. NASA is inviting the public to send their names aboard the agency’s Dragonfly rotorcraft and be part of the first science mission to fly and explore the surface of another world. To have your […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: NASA’s ISAM State of Play: The Industry Standard for Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing
item.description: When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligence, the team knew they had crossed an inflection point. “We’ve had some unnamed companies ask if we have any proprietary information,” says Dale Arney, senior team lead […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sondra Woodward

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Marks Way for Roman Space Telescope
item.description: A sweeping barred galaxy takes center stage in this Oct. 22, 2026, image, but the gravitational lensing at bottom right is the real target. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Astronomers will use these […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: ¿Puede la IA proteger a Internet de sus propias vulnerabilidades?
item.description: Dos vulnerabilidades críticas en PHP, el lenguaje de programación que utilizan millones de páginas web, encendieron las alarmas internacionales el pasado 21 de octubre. Los fallos, que habían pasado años sin que se demostrara su potencial de explotación, podían permitir a los atacantes tomar el control de servidores y acceder a información sensible. Investigadores de empresas independientes utilizaron modelos de inteligencia artificial para identificar y validar estas vulnerabilidades, lo que desencadenó una respuesta urgente de los responsables de PHP y de organismos de ciberseguridad. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Valentina T. Sánchez

item.title: The asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago may have also set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with scientists finding a surprising boost from so-called jumping genes hidden in ant DNA
item.description: Since the dinosaurs vanished, ants have flourished, with more than 15,000 species recognized globally. New research, spearheaded by Dr. Lukas Schrader, highlights the role of jumping genes in their evolution and resilience. Significant surges of these genes occurred during the early Paleogene period, enhancing ants' olfactory receptors and social communication skills, thus providing a genetic edge for survival in diverse environments. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula Lurks Within Sight of NASA’s Hubble, Webb
item.description: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details. Publicado también por: European Space Agency. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Museum specimens reveal shrinking flying foxes in Madagascar, with commercial hunting suspected
item.description: Flying foxes are the biggest bats in the world; they look like German shepherd puppies with 5-foot (1.5-meter) wingspans. But Madagascar's flying foxes are shrinking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient Alberta fish fossils reveal evolutionary secrets of modern species
item.description: Rare, complete fossils of ancient fish discovered in Alberta are helping fill in the gaps in our knowledge about which freshwater fish were living in North America at the end of the age of the dinosaurs, and how they evolved into their modern descendants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula lurks within sight of Hubble and Webb
item.description: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Modest gamma-ray flash followed by dazzling afterglow points to powerful stellar jet viewed off-axis
item.description: A cosmic explosion that announced itself with a modest flash of gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. An international team of astronomers now finds evidence that the surprising mismatch comes down to perspective: Earth was outside the most intensely beamed light from the explosion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indoor plants could improve air quality and cooling
item.description: In a study published in Eco-Environment and Health, a team of 35 international experts led by Surrey's Global Centre for Clean Air Research (GCARE) reviewed several studies from across the world on the performance of indoor greenery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jared Spiers
item.description: Jared Spiers had an interest in contributing to NASA’s mission long before becoming a civil servant for the agency. Growing up close to NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, and hearing about his father’s work there, he gained a firsthand connection to the nation’s space program. Before graduating high school, he knew […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: LaToya Dean

item.title: Using hydrogen to spark ammonia engines into life
item.description: "Ammonia was first used as a fuel during World War II, when gasoline was hard to get hold of," explains David Emberson, associate professor at NTNU's Department of Marine Technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Saharan dust carries desert bacteria across the Atlantic to Amazon rainforest
item.description: Viewed under a microscope, the air above the Amazon rainforest teems with activity. It is full of pollen, fungal spores, tiny plant particles and bacteria. Normally, the composition of this bioaerosol community is quite stable. A team that included researchers from the University of Graz, the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz and Brazilian partner institutions has now shown that microorganisms are transported across the Atlantic along with desert dust from the Sahara. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
item.description: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Children need to learn to swim for academic and social milestones, rather than just fitness, research suggests
item.description: With family budgets stretched ever tighter, swimming lessons can be one of the first expenses to be cut back—but with research showing swimming helps children not just physically but developmentally, researchers are calling for greater government support. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
item.description: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Struggling with your career? This psychological intervention may help
item.description: Job loss and career uncertainty can take a toll that extends well beyond the workplace. New research suggests that a psychological intervention based on the principles of acceptance and commitment therapy, or ACT, may help individuals navigate work-related challenges while improving well-being and reducing psychological distress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Amino acid boosts last-resort antibiotic's effectiveness
item.description: Worldwide, antibiotic resistance is associated with millions of deaths every year, and the World Health Organization warns that the number of resistant infections is rising. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used when other treatments fail, but rates of colistin-resistant infections are rising as well, putting people at even greater risk and increasing the urgency for new therapeutic approaches. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
item.description: A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
item.description: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Smaller ants devote more of their resting energy budget to their brains
item.description: The energy required for brains of different sizes to function could play a role in how different species evolved over time. While the energetic costs of brains have long been deemed important in evolution, direct measurements of the rate at which the brains of different species consume energy, also known as brain metabolic rates (MRs), remain scarce. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First individual-based model of basking sharks replicates complicated social and environmental drivers of behavior
item.description: A new study published in Individual-Based Ecology presents the first individual-based model (IBM) of basking shark behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
item.description: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How to keep electricity costs down amid uncertain federal policy
item.description: Keeping the lights on nationwide is a feat of engineering that depends on millions of miles of power lines and thousands of power-generation plants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
item.description: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Prosecutors invoke gender stereotypes in capital cases against women
item.description: In 2001, Brenda Andrew was convicted of murdering her husband, and in 2004 she was sentenced to death. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As ancient oceans warmed, carbon export and fish productivity surged
item.description: Ocean fish stocks have been increasingly exploited over time, and remote sensing shows they have declined in the open ocean over the last three decades, particularly in the tropics. But it's uncertain how fish populations will fare in the future, as climate models show both increases and decreases in global trends by the end of this century. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay
item.description: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit beyond its reputation for helping prevent urinary tract infections: protecting teeth from decay. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago discovered that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice slowed the regrowth of dental plaque bacteria and reduced their production of acids that damage tooth enamel. The secret may lie in naturally occurring compounds called proanthocyanidins, which interfere with harmful bacteria. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: American jobs offer more autonomy—and more stress
item.description: American jobs have become increasingly stressful over the past two decades—but workers have also gained greater ability to exercise independence and make decisions at work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Philippine island fights rising seas with nature, not concrete
item.description: For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 12 minutos: ese es el tiempo que necesitaría China para transmitir todo el conocimiento de la humanidad de 2007 utilizando esta fibra óptica de alta tecnología
item.description: China acaba de anunciar algo difícil de imaginar hace unos años: una velocidad de transmisión de datos de 3,2 petabits por segundo a través de una sola fibra óptica. Para entender la magnitud del experimento basta con una comparación. En 2007, la humanidad disponía de capacidad tecnológica para almacenar unos 295 exabytes de información, una cantidad equivalente a 315 veces el número estimado de granos de arena de la Tierra. Con la velocidad alcanzada por los investigadores chinos, transmitir ese volumen de datos requeriría minutos. Una humanidad entera en 12 minutos. Ocurrió el pasado 26 de… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
item.description: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: End of COVID-era SNAP emergency food assistance linked to increased child maltreatment rates
item.description: A new study has found that in U.S. counties that ended COVID-19 pandemic-era Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments, child maltreatment rates went up. The findings from the study in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine suggest that changes to food assistance programs have consequences that extend beyond food security and also affect child and family well-being. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
item.description: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
item.description: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
item.description: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy
item.description: Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Optimistic climate futures for local communities in the UK imagined in a new report
item.description: A new report co-authored by researchers from the University of York and WWF highlights how local communities across the U.K. imagine positive, sustainable, and resilient futures for the places where they live and work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
item.description: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How the Indian Ocean is linked to Europe's early-winter rain and storms
item.description: When we think about Europe's winter weather, the Indian Ocean is probably not the first place we look. We might picture Atlantic storms, cold air arriving from the north or rain sweeping across the Mediterranean. In my research, however, I look at how these familiar weather systems fit into a much larger climate system. My colleagues and I asked whether an ocean thousands of kilometers away could leave a detectable signature on Europe's early winter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4 The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: The phantom lighthouse: New research explains one of Australia's strangest illusions
item.description: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The first was built in 1873, but was decommissioned in 1995 when the second took over the job of warning ships off the reef. Visitors to the island, however, regularly report seeing signs of a third lighthouse. At night the beams of a nonexistent phantom lighthouse are seen far off, shining on the horizon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
item.description: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
item.description: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
item.description: This Vulcan launch will be the first to utilize a full complement of six solid rocket boosters. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
item.description: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
item.description: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
item.description: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
item.description: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space. “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
item.description: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
item.description: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
item.description: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
item.description: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon‑stealing spirits
item.description: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
item.description: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
item.description: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
item.description: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
item.description: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New tissue atlas aims to help AI understand cancer
item.description: How cells are arranged within tissue can reveal as much about disease as the cells themselves. When doctors examine a cancer tumor, for example, they don't just look at which cells are present; they also want to know how those cells are arranged and how they interact with each other. That's because the way cancer cells interact with neighboring immune cells can offer important clues about how a disease develops or responds to treatment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
item.description: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way. Fuente: Phys.org.
